script.opening: (Tired, frustrated, a little tearful; holds her left side.) "Doctor, the shingles rash cleared up months ago, so I don't understand it — the skin on my left side still burns and stabs, day and night. Even my nightie touching it is agony. The paracetamol and ibuprofen do nothing. I'm not sleeping, I'm worn out, and I'm starting to wonder if it'll ever go. Is something else wrong?"

facts.text: "Just here, round the left side under my breast to my back. Exactly where the blisters were." Burning all the time, with sudden stabbing jolts several times an hour. Will trace the band on camera.
"No, it looks normal now. It just hurts when anything touches it." Light touch, clothes and bedsheets hurt more than firm pressure. No new rash, no blisters.

"No, nothing like that. I'm eating fine. It's just this band." No weight loss, no fevers, no weakness in the legs, no bladder or bowel change, no back pain apart from the band, no chest pain with exertion or breathlessness.

"The usual doses from the packet. My stomach's fine, but they don't touch it, so I sometimes don't bother." Paracetamol 1 g up to four times a day and ibuprofen 400 mg three times a day, bought herself. Didn't get antivirals at the time — "I didn't see anyone till the rash was crusting."

Hypertension — ramipril 5 mg. Mild osteoarthritis of the knees. If asked: "No falls. I'm not aware of anything wrong with my kidneys." No glaucoma, no heart rhythm problems, no urinary retention. No allergies. Has not had the shingles vaccine.

"I'm not sleeping. I'm worn out, and I feel low. I don't go out as much because I can't bear clothes rubbing on it." If asked about self-harm: "Low, yes, and fed up. But nothing like that — I just want to sleep."
Widow, lives alone in a bungalow, daughter visits weekly. Used to go to the church lunch club; stopped. Non-smoker, a small sherry at weekends. Doesn't drive.

"I don't want anything that makes me groggy" — worried about falling at night. If offered a choice and told duloxetine can help mood too: "The low mood is part of it. I'd try the duloxetine." Happy to try a cream: "I'll try anything that stops the nightie hurting."

Weary and confused about why it still hurts. If asked what she fears: "If the shingles is gone, why is it still hurting? I thought it might be something serious underneath. And I'm starting to think it'll never go." Relieved by a clear explanation: "So it's the nerve, not the skin? … I felt I was doing something wrong."

ice.ideas: "The shingles has gone, so something else must be wrong."
ice.concerns: That it will never go away, or that something serious is hidden underneath; exhaustion and low mood; becoming housebound.
ice.expectations: "Something that actually works. And to know it isn't something worse."

cues: "Even my nightie touching it is agony." — allodynia; invites explaining nerve pain.
"I don't go out as much." — isolation to explore.

checkpoints.text: Recognises POSTHERPETIC NEURALGIA (neuropathic pain 90 days or more after rash onset in the dermatome: burning/stabbing, allodynia, hyperalgesia) and reassures it is a recognised after-effect, briefly excluding atypical features
Explains why paracetamol/NSAIDs are largely INEFFECTIVE for neuropathic pain — reframing the "nothing works" as a need for neuropathic agents, not patient failure

Institutes the NICE CG173 neuropathic ladder: a first-line choice of amitriptyline, duloxetine, gabapentin or pregabalin — one at a time, started low and TITRATED (doses per BNF), switching to one of the remaining three if ineffective/intolerable — tailored to the elderly patient’s comorbidity and risks

Offers TOPICAL options suited to localised pain/allodynia in an older patient (capsaicin cream per CG173; lidocaine 5% plasters are licensed for PHN but not recommended by CG173, so only as the local formulary allows) and considers sleep, physiotherapy/psychological support, and pain-clinic referral if refractory

AVOIDS the pitfalls — no long-term opioids (CG173: tramadol only as acute rescue; no other opioids started without specialist advice), no endless escalation of paracetamol/NSAIDs, mindful of polypharmacy/falls/sedation in the elderly — and sets REALISTIC expectations (partial relief, weeks to work)
Explores and validates the bio-psycho-social toll (sleep, mood, function, isolation), screens low mood, and treats the whole person rather than just prescribing
Reassures about the confusing "rash gone but pain remains", checks understanding of the medication plan and titration, and addresses her fear that it will never resolve honestly

Safety-nets and follows up: titration/review plan with realistic timeframe and side-effect counselling, sleep/mood support, what to report, pain-clinic referral if refractory, and mention of shingles vaccination for the future (Green Book chapter 28a: Shingrix for 70–79-year-olds) — active neuropathic management, not "nothing to be done"

worked.txt: "Let me explain what’s going on, because it IS confusing. Shingles can damage the nerve it travels along, and that nerve can keep firing pain signals long after the rash heals — we call it postherpetic neuralgia. It’s a known after-effect, not a sign something new is wrong."

"And here’s why the paracetamol and ibuprofen did nothing — they’re the wrong tools. This is nerve pain, and nerve pain needs a completely different kind of medicine. So you haven’t failed; we’ve just not used the right treatment yet."

"There are a few good options — tablets like amitriptyline, duloxetine, gabapentin or pregabalin. We pick one, start low, build it up slowly, and give it a few weeks. The honest aim is to take the edge off — better sleep, less burning — rather than zero pain overnight. If one doesn’t suit you, we switch."

"Because even your nightie hurts, a cream applied to that band of skin can help directly, with fewer effects on the rest of you — useful at your age. There’s also a numbing plaster that’s licensed for this; the NICE CG173 guideline doesn’t recommend it routinely, so it depends on our local prescribing rules. We can use a cream alongside a tablet."

"This has clearly worn you down — the sleep, your mood. That matters as much as the pain itself, and treating the pain should help, but tell me how you’re doing in yourself … I want to look after the whole picture, not just the skin."

"Let’s start one tablet and review you in a couple of weeks to adjust the dose. If side-effects trouble you — drowsiness, dizziness — tell me rather than stopping. If we can’t settle it, there’s a pain clinic. And for the future, the shingles vaccine lowers the chance of this happening again."

f.learning: POSTHERPETIC NEURALGIA (PHN) is neuropathic pain persisting in the affected dermatome 90 days or more after the shingles rash began (timed from rash onset; Dworkin 2007, international) — burning, stabbing or electric-shock pain with ALLODYNIA (pain from light touch such as clothing/bedsheets), hyperalgesia and itch — with risk rising with age. Recognise it, reassure that it is a known after-effect rather than a new disease (excluding atypical features), and — crucially — explain why ordinary analgesics fail: paracetamol and NSAIDs target nociceptive/inflammatory pain and are largely ineffective for neuropathic pain, so "nothing works" reflects the wrong tool, not patient failure. Institute the NICE CG173 neuropathic pain ladder (2013, updated 2020): offer a first-line CHOICE of amitriptyline, duloxetine, gabapentin or pregabalin, one at a time, started low and titrated, with realistic expectations (meaningful relief and improved sleep/function built over weeks, rather than zero pain), switching to one of the remaining first-line agents if ineffective or intolerable and tailoring choice to comorbidity and elderly-specific risks (anticholinergic/falls/sedation; gabapentinoid sedation/dependence — Schedule 3 controlled drugs, MHRA Drug Safety Update April 2019, with respiratory depression risk alongside opioids, MHRA October 2017). Add TOPICAL options well-suited to localised pain and allodynia in older people (capsaicin cream per CG173; lidocaine 5% plasters are licensed for PHN but not recommended by CG173, so only as the local formulary allows), address sleep and consider physiotherapy/psychological support and pain-clinic referral if refractory. Avoid long-term opioids (CG173: tramadol only as acute rescue; no other opioids started in non-specialist settings without specialist advice), endless escalation of paracetamol/NSAIDs, and polypharmacy harms. Address the bio-psycho-social toll — sleep, mood, function, isolation — validate it, treat the whole person, and mention shingles VACCINATION for prevention (UKHSA Green Book chapter 28a: Shingrix for adults aged 70 to 79).

knowledge.guideline: NICE CG173 (neuropathic pain in adults, 2013, updated 2020) · UKHSA Green Book chapter 28a (shingles) · MHRA Drug Safety Update (April 2019; October 2017) · BNF
knowledge.summary: Burning dermatomal pain with allodynia months after shingles is postherpetic neuralgia. Stop what is not working, offer one CG173 first-line neuropathic agent at a time, tailor it to a 74-year-old, and look after sleep and mood.

points.t: Postherpetic neuralgia is pain in the affected dermatome persisting 90 days or more after the rash began (Dworkin 2007, international). Burning or stabbing pain, allodynia to clothing and itch in the T6 band fit. Check the skin and the pattern are typical before labelling.

Simple analgesics act on nociceptive and inflammatory pain and help neuropathic pain little. Stop ibuprofen if it gives no benefit: in a 74-year-old it carries gastrointestinal, renal and cardiovascular risk for no gain.

NICE CG173: offer a choice of amitriptyline, duloxetine, gabapentin or pregabalin. If the first is ineffective or not tolerated, offer one of the remaining three, and switch again if needed. One drug at a time, start low, titrate, doses per BNF. Review early for side effects and dose, then regularly.

Amitriptyline: anticholinergic effects, sedation and falls risk in older people (BNF). Gabapentin and pregabalin: Schedule 3 controlled drugs since April 2019 for abuse and dependence risk (MHRA Drug Safety Update, April 2019); respiratory depression risk rises with opioids (MHRA Drug Safety Update, October 2017); adjust for renal function per BNF. Duloxetine: avoid with hepatic impairment (BNF) and consider it if low mood coexists.

NICE CG173: consider capsaicin cream for localised neuropathic pain in people who wish to avoid, or cannot tolerate, oral treatment. Lidocaine 5% plasters are licensed for postherpetic neuralgia but CG173 does not recommend them; use only as the local formulary allows.

NICE CG173: tramadol only as acute rescue; do not start other opioids for neuropathic pain in non-specialist settings without specialist advice. Refer to a pain service if pain stays severe or limits daily life despite first-line options.
UKHSA Green Book chapter 28a: Shingrix is offered to adults aged 70 to 79 until their 80th birthday, as two doses. She is eligible; check the chapter for timing after a recent episode.

model.text: Hello Mrs Caldwell, I’m Dr Lee. I can see you had shingles a few months ago. Tell me in your own words what has been happening since.
The rash cleared months ago, but my left side still burns and stabs, day and night. Even my nightie touching it is agony. The paracetamol and ibuprofen do nothing. Is something else wrong?

That sounds exhausting, and I can hear how worrying it is that it hasn’t gone. I’d like to understand the pain properly, check for anything unusual, and then explain what I think it is and what will help. Does that suit you?
model.why: Acknowledges distress and sets a clear agenda

model.text: Yes, please. I just want to know what’s going on.
Can you show me on yourself where the pain is? Does it stay in the same band where the rash was?
Just here, round the left side under my breast to my back. Exactly where the blisters were.
And the skin itself — any new rash, lumps, colour change, or blisters coming back?
model.why: Screens for atypical features and recurrence

model.text: No, it looks normal now. It just hurts when anything touches it.
Any weakness, numbness spreading elsewhere, weight loss, fevers or new back pain that feels different from this burning?
model.why: Excludes other causes of thoracic pain

model.text: No, nothing like that. I’m eating fine. It’s just this band.
How much paracetamol and ibuprofen have you been taking, and has your stomach been all right with it?
model.why: Checks analgesic use and NSAID harm

model.text: The usual doses from the packet. My stomach’s fine, but they don’t touch it, so I sometimes don’t bother.
You said you wondered whether something else is wrong. What have you been worrying it might be?
model.why: Picks up her opening cue and explores the idea

model.text: If the shingles is gone, why is it still hurting? I thought it might be something serious underneath. And I’m starting to think it’ll never go.
Thank you for telling me. How is this affecting you day to day — your sleep, your mood, getting out?
I’m not sleeping. I’m worn out, and I feel low. I don’t go out as much because I can’t bear clothes rubbing on it.
That’s a lot to be carrying. Over the last couple of weeks, have you felt down most days, or lost interest in things you used to enjoy? Any thoughts that life isn’t worth living?
Low, yes, and fed up. But nothing like that — I just want to sleep.
And what were you hoping we could do today?
Something that actually works. And to know it isn’t something worse.

Everything you describe fits a known after-effect of shingles called postherpetic neuralgia. The virus irritates the nerve, and the nerve can carry on sending pain signals after the skin has healed. It isn’t a new illness, and nothing you’ve told me suggests something else underneath.
model.why: Names the diagnosis and answers her fear

model.text: So it’s the nerve, not the skin?

Exactly. And that’s why the paracetamol and ibuprofen didn’t help: they’re aimed at a different kind of pain. You haven’t failed with them — they’re the wrong tool. I’d stop the ibuprofen, because at your age it can upset the stomach and kidneys without doing any good here.
model.why: Explains analgesic failure and stops a harmful drug

model.text: That makes sense. I felt I was doing something wrong.

Nerve pain has its own medicines. There are four we usually start with: amitriptyline, duloxetine, gabapentin and pregabalin. We try one at a time, start small and build up slowly. Some suit older people better than others — can I ask a couple of things to help choose?
Go on.
Have you had any falls or dizziness, and how are your kidneys and liver, as far as you know? Some of these can make people drowsy or unsteady, which matters at night.
model.why: Tailors choice to falls, renal and hepatic risk

model.text: No falls. I’m not aware of anything wrong with my kidneys. I don’t want anything that makes me groggy.

Then here are the trade-offs. Duloxetine can help mood as well as nerve pain. Gabapentin or pregabalin can help sleep but may cause drowsiness. Amitriptyline at night helps sleep but is more likely to cause dry mouth and unsteadiness at your age. Which feels right to you?
The low mood is part of it. I’d try the duloxetine.

A good choice. I’ll start a low dose and we’ll adjust it. Nausea and dizziness can happen early and often settle. It takes a few weeks to work, and the aim is to take the edge off and help you sleep, rather than no pain at all. If it doesn’t suit you, we switch to another.

Because clothes touching the skin is so painful, a capsaicin cream on that band is another option alongside or instead. It can sting at first. And a soft cotton layer next to the skin can help in the meantime.
I’ll try anything that stops the nightie hurting.

I’ll speak to you again in about two weeks to see how you’re getting on and adjust the dose. If you get a new rash, weakness, a fever, or you ever feel you can’t cope or life isn’t worth living, contact us the same day. If we can’t get on top of it, there’s a pain clinic.
model.why: Defined review, red flags and escalation

model.text: One more thing for later: you’re eligible for the shingles vaccine, which lowers the chance of shingles again. We’ll talk about timing when this settles. To check I’ve explained it well — what will you tell a friend about why it still hurts?
That the nerve is still upset after the shingles, and I need a nerve medicine, not ordinary painkillers. And a cream. I feel better knowing what it is.

social.t: Chronic pain and poor sleep can shrink an older person’s world. Ask how she manages at home and whether she is going out less, and offer support rather than only a prescription.
Low mood is common with persistent pain. Screen for depression and ask about risk (NICE NG222); treating the pain and sleep often lifts mood, but depression needs its own plan if present.

legal.t: If she drives, advise her not to drive if a new drug makes her drowsy or dizzy. Gabapentin and pregabalin are Schedule 3 controlled drugs (MHRA Drug Safety Update, April 2019).

professional.t: Start low, go slow, review early, and record why a drug was chosen. Check the whole medication list for sedative and anticholinergic burden (GMC Good medical practice, 2024: prescribe safely).
Offer the first-line options with their trade-offs and let her choose; document the discussion and the review plan.

community.t: Shingrix via the NHS shingles programme for eligible ages (UKHSA Green Book chapter 28a); practice nurse or community pharmacy can help with booking where offered locally.
Community pain management programmes and physiotherapy where available; pain clinic referral if first-line options fail.

redFlags: New rash, blistering or spreading lesions — possible recurrence
Weakness, sensory loss beyond the dermatome, sphincter change or new severe back pain — look for another cause
Weight loss, fevers or night sweats — do not assume postherpetic neuralgia
Low mood with thoughts that life is not worth living
psychosocial: Sleep lost to night-time pain and allodynia
Low mood and going out less because clothes hurt
Falls risk and sedation worries with new medicines
ice: Idea: “If the shingles is gone, something else must be wrong”
Concern: it will never go; exhaustion and low mood
Expectation: a treatment that actually works and reassurance

playbook.diagnosis: Postherpetic neuralgia: persistent neuropathic pain with allodynia in the left T6 dermatome four months after shingles, with no atypical features. Simple analgesics are ineffective for this type of pain.
playbook.diagnosisLay: “Shingles is a virus that travels along a nerve. It can leave the nerve irritated, so it keeps sending pain messages after the skin has healed — like a faulty alarm that keeps ringing after the danger has gone.”

management.reflectIce: “You were worried something else was going on. From everything you’ve told me, this is the nerve still upset after shingles — and it’s treatable.”
management.psychosocial: Address sleep and mood alongside pain; suggest soft cotton next to the skin; check how she is coping at home and whether she is going out less.
sharedPlan: Stop ibuprofen; explain simple analgesics are the wrong tool
One NICE CG173 first-line agent (her choice: duloxetine), started low and titrated per BNF
Consider capsaicin cream for the localised allodynia
Switch to another first-line agent if ineffective or not tolerated; pain clinic if refractory
safetyNet: Review in about two weeks to check side effects and adjust dose
Same-day contact for new rash, weakness, fever or thoughts of self-harm
Shingrix discussion once this has settled

pitfalls.intro: This station is failed less on drug names than on treating the pain as ordinary, ignoring her fear and mood, and prescribing without a plan. The patterns below are common and fixable.

items.fail: Escalating to co-codamol or tramadol because “the paracetamol isn’t strong enough”.
items.why: Neuropathic pain responds poorly to simple analgesics and opioids; NICE CG173 limits tramadol to acute rescue. Examiners read this as not recognising the diagnosis.
items.fix: Name postherpetic neuralgia and switch class: offer a choice of amitriptyline, duloxetine, gabapentin or pregabalin.

items.fail: Prescribing amitriptyline by habit without asking about falls, dizziness or other medicines in a 74-year-old.
items.why: Anticholinergic and sedative effects raise falls risk in older people. A plan that ignores her age is not safe.
items.fix: Ask about falls, renal and hepatic history, then lay out the trade-offs and let her choose.

items.fail: Hearing “is something else wrong?” and moving straight to drug choice.
items.why: Her main fear is unaddressed, so reassurance later lands poorly. “Does not respond to the patient’s cues” is standard failing feedback.
items.fix: Return to it: “You wondered if something else is going on — let me tell you why I don’t think so.”

items.fail: Never asking about sleep or mood despite “I’m worn out”.
items.why: The bio-psycho-social toll is half this case. Missing low mood and risk is a Relating and a safety failure.
items.fix: Ask directly about mood and thoughts of self-harm, and let the answer shape the drug choice.

items.fail: Starting a new drug with “see how you get on” and no review.
items.why: These drugs need titration and early side-effect checks. Vague follow-up is marked as unsafe.
items.fix: Give a named review in about two weeks, what side effects to expect, and when to call sooner.

items.fail: Promising the tablet will make the pain go away.
items.why: Unrealistic expectations lead to early stopping and loss of trust.
items.fix: “The aim is to take the edge off and help you sleep; it takes a few weeks and we adjust as we go.”

Distribution, allodynia, skin now, atypical features (weight loss, weakness, fever), analgesic use and NSAID harm.
Her fear of something serious, sleep, mood (ask about risk), going out less.

wordPics.fail: Increases the paracetamol or adds codeine; never names postherpetic neuralgia; starts a neuropathic drug without explaining titration or side effects; ignores sleep and low mood; no review date.
wordPics.pass: Names postherpetic neuralgia and explains why simple analgesics failed; offers one CG173 first-line drug with a titration plan; asks about mood; books a review with basic safety-netting.
wordPics.exc: All of that, plus: answers her fear that something else is wrong; weighs falls, sedation and renal cautions and lets her choose; stops the ibuprofen; offers capsaicin cream for the allodynia; screens risk; mentions Shingrix; checks understanding with teach-back.

avoid.dont: “Shingles pain can take a while — just keep taking the painkillers.”
avoid.instead: “This is nerve pain, and ordinary painkillers aren’t built for it. Let’s use a medicine that is.”
avoid.why: Leaves her on drugs that do not work and dismisses four months of suffering.

avoid.dont: “I’ll give you some codeine to take the edge off.”
avoid.instead: “Strong painkillers don’t help this kind of pain much and cause falls and constipation. There are better options.”
avoid.why: NICE CG173 does not support opioids for ongoing neuropathic pain in primary care.

avoid.dont: “This tablet should get rid of the pain.”
avoid.instead: “The aim is to take the edge off and help you sleep. It takes a few weeks, and we adjust as we go.”
avoid.why: Over-promising sets her up to feel she has failed again.

SCA_MODELS.text: If the shingles is gone, why is it still hurting? I thought it might be something serious underneath. And I’m starting to think it’ll never go.
Thank you for telling me. How is this affecting you day to day — your sleep, your mood, getting out?
I’m not sleeping. I’m worn out, and I feel low. I don’t go out as much because I can’t bear clothes rubbing on it.
That’s a lot to be carrying. Over the last couple of weeks, have you felt down most days, or lost interest in things you used to enjoy? Any thoughts that life isn’t worth living?
Low, yes, and fed up. But nothing like that — I just want to sleep.
And what were you hoping we could do today?
Something that actually works. And to know it isn’t something worse.

Everything you describe fits a known after-effect of shingles called postherpetic neuralgia. The virus irritates the nerve, and the nerve can carry on sending pain signals after the skin has healed. It isn’t a new illness, and nothing you’ve told me suggests something else underneath.
SCA_MODELS.why: Names the diagnosis and answers her fear

SCA_MODELS.text: So it’s the nerve, not the skin?

Exactly. And that’s why the paracetamol and ibuprofen didn’t help: they’re aimed at a different kind of pain. You haven’t failed with them — they’re the wrong tool. I’d stop the ibuprofen, because at your age it can upset the stomach and kidneys without doing any good here.
SCA_MODELS.why: Explains analgesic failure and stops a harmful drug

SCA_MODELS.text: That makes sense. I felt I was doing something wrong.

Nerve pain has its own medicines. There are four we usually start with: amitriptyline, duloxetine, gabapentin and pregabalin. We try one at a time, start small and build up slowly. Some suit older people better than others — can I ask a couple of things to help choose?
Go on.
Have you had any falls or dizziness, and how are your kidneys and liver, as far as you know? Some of these can make people drowsy or unsteady, which matters at night.
SCA_MODELS.why: Tailors choice to falls, renal and hepatic risk

SCA_MODELS.text: No falls. I’m not aware of anything wrong with my kidneys. I don’t want anything that makes me groggy.

Then here are the trade-offs. Duloxetine can help mood as well as nerve pain. Gabapentin or pregabalin can help sleep but may cause drowsiness. Amitriptyline at night helps sleep but is more likely to cause dry mouth and unsteadiness at your age. Which feels right to you?
The low mood is part of it. I’d try the duloxetine.

A good choice. I’ll start a low dose and we’ll adjust it. Nausea and dizziness can happen early and often settle. It takes a few weeks to work, and the aim is to take the edge off and help you sleep, rather than no pain at all. If it doesn’t suit you, we switch to another.

Because clothes touching the skin is so painful, a capsaicin cream on that band is another option alongside or instead. It can sting at first. And a soft cotton layer next to the skin can help in the meantime.
I’ll try anything that stops the nightie hurting.

I’ll speak to you again in about two weeks to see how you’re getting on and adjust the dose. If you get a new rash, weakness, a fever, or you ever feel you can’t cope or life isn’t worth living, contact us the same day. If we can’t get on top of it, there’s a pain clinic.
SCA_MODELS.why: Defined review, red flags and escalation

SCA_MODELS.text: One more thing for later: you’re eligible for the shingles vaccine, which lowers the chance of shingles again. We’ll talk about timing when this settles. To check I’ve explained it well — what will you tell a friend about why it still hurts?
That the nerve is still upset after the shingles, and I need a nerve medicine, not ordinary painkillers. And a cream. I feel better knowing what it is.

SCA_STEM.name: Edith Caldwell
pmh: Shingles, left T6 dermatome, four months ago — rash healed
Persistent pain in the same band since
SCA_STEM.recent: Shingles episode four months ago, left T6. Rash has cleared. Reports ongoing burning, stabbing pain in the same band, clothing and bedsheets painful to touch, poor sleep.
SCA_STEM.reason: Video consultation about pain that has continued since her shingles healed.

SCA_KNOWLEDGE.guideline: NICE CG173 (neuropathic pain in adults, 2013, updated 2020) · UKHSA Green Book chapter 28a (shingles) · MHRA Drug Safety Update (April 2019; October 2017) · BNF
SCA_KNOWLEDGE.summary: Burning dermatomal pain with allodynia months after shingles is postherpetic neuralgia. Stop what is not working, offer one CG173 first-line neuropathic agent at a time, tailor it to a 74-year-old, and look after sleep and mood.

points.t: Postherpetic neuralgia is pain in the affected dermatome persisting 90 days or more after the rash began (Dworkin 2007, international). Burning or stabbing pain, allodynia to clothing and itch in the T6 band fit. Check the skin and the pattern are typical before labelling.

Simple analgesics act on nociceptive and inflammatory pain and help neuropathic pain little. Stop ibuprofen if it gives no benefit: in a 74-year-old it carries gastrointestinal, renal and cardiovascular risk for no gain.

NICE CG173: offer a choice of amitriptyline, duloxetine, gabapentin or pregabalin. If the first is ineffective or not tolerated, offer one of the remaining three, and switch again if needed. One drug at a time, start low, titrate, doses per BNF. Review early for side effects and dose, then regularly.

Amitriptyline: anticholinergic effects, sedation and falls risk in older people (BNF). Gabapentin and pregabalin: Schedule 3 controlled drugs since April 2019 for abuse and dependence risk (MHRA Drug Safety Update, April 2019); respiratory depression risk rises with opioids (MHRA Drug Safety Update, October 2017); adjust for renal function per BNF. Duloxetine: avoid with hepatic impairment (BNF) and consider it if low mood coexists.

NICE CG173: consider capsaicin cream for localised neuropathic pain in people who wish to avoid, or cannot tolerate, oral treatment. Lidocaine 5% plasters are licensed for postherpetic neuralgia but CG173 does not recommend them; use only as the local formulary allows.

NICE CG173: tramadol only as acute rescue; do not start other opioids for neuropathic pain in non-specialist settings without specialist advice. Refer to a pain service if pain stays severe or limits daily life despite first-line options.
UKHSA Green Book chapter 28a: Shingrix is offered to adults aged 70 to 79 until their 80th birthday, as two doses. She is eligible; check the chapter for timing after a recent episode.

SCA_SC_TASKS.d: Open question; let her describe the burning, the band and the failed painkillers before focusing.
Sleep, mood, going out less because clothing hurts, and how she manages at home.
Picked up “is something else wrong?” and “I’m worn out” and explored both.
Idea (something serious underneath), concern (it will never go; exhaustion), expectation (treatment that works).
Inspect the T6 band at a face-to-face review; check renal function before gabapentinoids if not recent; mood screen.
Postherpetic neuralgia vs recurrence, other thoracic or spinal causes; screened for weight loss, weakness and fever.
No atypical skin change, neurology or systemic features; low mood and risk asked about directly.
Named postherpetic neuralgia in plain words and explained why simple analgesics failed.
NICE CG173 first-line choice, one drug at a time, started low and titrated; capsaicin cream considered; ibuprofen stopped.
Falls, sedation, renal and hepatic cautions weighed; duloxetine chosen with low mood in mind.
Review in about two weeks, side effects named, pain clinic if refractory, mood crisis advice, Shingrix discussed.

social.t: Chronic pain and poor sleep can shrink an older person’s world. Ask how she manages at home and whether she is going out less, and offer support rather than only a prescription.
Low mood is common with persistent pain. Screen for depression and ask about risk (NICE NG222); treating the pain and sleep often lifts mood, but depression needs its own plan if present.

legal.t: If she drives, advise her not to drive if a new drug makes her drowsy or dizzy. Gabapentin and pregabalin are Schedule 3 controlled drugs (MHRA Drug Safety Update, April 2019).

professional.t: Start low, go slow, review early, and record why a drug was chosen. Check the whole medication list for sedative and anticholinergic burden (GMC Good medical practice, 2024: prescribe safely).
Offer the first-line options with their trade-offs and let her choose; document the discussion and the review plan.

community.t: Shingrix via the NHS shingles programme for eligible ages (UKHSA Green Book chapter 28a); practice nurse or community pharmacy can help with booking where offered locally.
Community pain management programmes and physiotherapy where available; pain clinic referral if first-line options fail.

redFlags: New rash, blistering or spreading lesions — possible recurrence
Weakness, sensory loss beyond the dermatome, sphincter change or new severe back pain — look for another cause
Weight loss, fevers or night sweats — do not assume postherpetic neuralgia
Low mood with thoughts that life is not worth living
psychosocial: Sleep lost to night-time pain and allodynia
Low mood and going out less because clothes hurt
Falls risk and sedation worries with new medicines
ice: Idea: “If the shingles is gone, something else must be wrong”
Concern: it will never go; exhaustion and low mood
Expectation: a treatment that actually works and reassurance

SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosis: Postherpetic neuralgia: persistent neuropathic pain with allodynia in the left T6 dermatome four months after shingles, with no atypical features. Simple analgesics are ineffective for this type of pain.
SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosisLay: “Shingles is a virus that travels along a nerve. It can leave the nerve irritated, so it keeps sending pain messages after the skin has healed — like a faulty alarm that keeps ringing after the danger has gone.”

management.reflectIce: “You were worried something else was going on. From everything you’ve told me, this is the nerve still upset after shingles — and it’s treatable.”
management.psychosocial: Address sleep and mood alongside pain; suggest soft cotton next to the skin; check how she is coping at home and whether she is going out less.
sharedPlan: Stop ibuprofen; explain simple analgesics are the wrong tool
One NICE CG173 first-line agent (her choice: duloxetine), started low and titrated per BNF
Consider capsaicin cream for the localised allodynia
Switch to another first-line agent if ineffective or not tolerated; pain clinic if refractory
safetyNet: Review in about two weeks to check side effects and adjust dose
Same-day contact for new rash, weakness, fever or thoughts of self-harm
Shingrix discussion once this has settled

SCA_PITFALLS.intro: This station is failed less on drug names than on treating the pain as ordinary, ignoring her fear and mood, and prescribing without a plan. The patterns below are common and fixable.

items.fail: Escalating to co-codamol or tramadol because “the paracetamol isn’t strong enough”.
items.why: Neuropathic pain responds poorly to simple analgesics and opioids; NICE CG173 limits tramadol to acute rescue. Examiners read this as not recognising the diagnosis.
items.fix: Name postherpetic neuralgia and switch class: offer a choice of amitriptyline, duloxetine, gabapentin or pregabalin.

items.fail: Prescribing amitriptyline by habit without asking about falls, dizziness or other medicines in a 74-year-old.
items.why: Anticholinergic and sedative effects raise falls risk in older people. A plan that ignores her age is not safe.
items.fix: Ask about falls, renal and hepatic history, then lay out the trade-offs and let her choose.

items.fail: Hearing “is something else wrong?” and moving straight to drug choice.
items.why: Her main fear is unaddressed, so reassurance later lands poorly. “Does not respond to the patient’s cues” is standard failing feedback.
items.fix: Return to it: “You wondered if something else is going on — let me tell you why I don’t think so.”

items.fail: Never asking about sleep or mood despite “I’m worn out”.
items.why: The bio-psycho-social toll is half this case. Missing low mood and risk is a Relating and a safety failure.
items.fix: Ask directly about mood and thoughts of self-harm, and let the answer shape the drug choice.

items.fail: Starting a new drug with “see how you get on” and no review.
items.why: These drugs need titration and early side-effect checks. Vague follow-up is marked as unsafe.
items.fix: Give a named review in about two weeks, what side effects to expect, and when to call sooner.

items.fail: Promising the tablet will make the pain go away.
items.why: Unrealistic expectations lead to early stopping and loss of trust.
items.fix: “The aim is to take the edge off and help you sleep; it takes a few weeks and we adjust as we go.”
